title: Charting America's Marriage Deserts and Gardens
gist: Chris Bullivant and Ken Burchfiel summarize a new IFS report mapping US 'marriage deserts' and 'gardens' with 2020 Census PUMA data. In the lowest-marriage areas only 13-17% of householders aged 15-64 are married, compared with 74-79% in the highest. Deserts cluster in urban cores such as Lower Manhattan/Brooklyn, while gardens are in affluent suburbs such as Dallas-Fort Worth and the DC-to-Philadelphia corridor.

insights.claim: A new IFS report uses 2020 Census data for Public Use Microdata Areas (100,000-200,000 people each) to measure two things: the share of householders aged 15-64 who are married, and the share of households with children headed by married couples.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies

insights.claim: In the US, higher marriage rates are found mainly in suburbs and lower marriage rates in the centers of major cities.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Married households concentrate in the suburbs, which supports demand for suburban family housing.
insights.quote: Higher marriage rates tend to be found in suburban regions, whereas lower marriage rates are often found in the center of major cities.

insights.claim: In the 10 lowest-marriage US PUMAs, only about 13% to 17% of householders aged 15-64 are married, compared with 74% to 79% in the largest marriage gardens.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: The roughly 60-point gap shows family structure is sharply polarized by geography.

insights.claim: In the top US married-family deserts, only about 18% to 26% of households with children are headed by married couples, compared with about 86% to 89% in the top married-family gardens, which tend to be in affluent suburbs.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Children's family stability is tied to neighborhood affluence, which reinforces inequality in human capital.
insights.quote: in the top married-family deserts, only around 18% to 26% of households with children are headed by married couples

insights.claim: Married-couple-led households with children are less common in US urban centers and parts of the Southeast.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: The Southeast's growing population includes areas of low family stability, which affects regional demand for social spending.

insights.claim: The largest contiguous US marriage desert, covering Lower Manhattan and Brooklyn, has over 686,000 householders aged 15-64, while the largest marriage garden, in the Dallas-Fort Worth suburbs, has over 630,000.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: New York's urban core and Texas suburbs represent opposite household-formation markets of similar size.

insights.claim: The largest contiguous US married-family desert, in Manhattan and the Bronx, has about 178,000 households with children, while the largest married-family garden, running from the DC suburbs to the Philadelphia suburbs, has about 386,000.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: The Northeast corridor contains both extremes of family structure close together, within the same labor markets.

insights.claim: IFS suggests newlyweds can use the marriage-garden maps to find areas with many other married couples and potentially stronger community support networks.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Married couples choosing where to live based on family density could reinforce suburban sorting.
